title: The great collections, closed
hookLine: the Connected and the Numbered Sayings

cards: Long discourses are like novels. These two libraries are more like a box of letters: a question asked at a roadside, an image tossed off before a meal, a list counted on the fingers.
The Samyutta Nikaya, the Connected Sayings. The Anguttara Nikaya, the Numbered Sayings. Together they hold thousands of short discourses, many no longer than a page.

Forty-five days ago this part of the path opened them. Since then you've crossed the flood, seen Mara named, taken apart a chariot, felt the second arrow, watched foam on the river, and pulled your ears.

teach.b: Start with how they're built, because that's today's line. The Connected Sayings gathers its suttas by kind: fifty-six groups, each on one theme or one speaker.
A chapter of verses with gods, a chapter on Mara, one on the five aggregates, one on the sense bases, one on mindfulness. Read it and you see a subject turned over a hundred ways.
That's where you met the chariot of parts, the burden, the dog on its leash, all is burning, the eye as an ocean, the nuns and the inspiring sign, and the old Buddha in the sun.
The Numbered Sayings gathers its suttas by number: the Book of Ones, the Book of Twos, all the way up to Elevens. Three intoxications. Four kinds of people, and the firebrand.
Five remembrances. Five ways to remove a grudge.
Six ways to be dear. Seven marks of a friend. Eight winds.
Ten perceptions at a sick bed. Eleven blessings of metta.

Why sort teaching by number? Tradition says these texts were passed on by memory, chanted by monks for generations before they were written down, and a list of five is easier to carry than a paragraph.
By kind, you go deep into one subject. By number, you get a toolkit to count on your fingers on an ordinary Tuesday.
And across both, the same teacher speaks to monks and nuns, kings and farmers, couples and the sick, in the plainest images he could find.

how: Monastics in the Theravada tradition still memorize and chant suttas from the Connected and Numbered Sayings, and some lay study groups read them one short discourse at a time.

games.q: the great collections: tap the pairs.

s: the Numbered Sayings run from the Book of Ones to the Book of Elevens
eleven books, each gathering teachings with that many items.
the Connected Sayings are sorted by length
they're grouped by theme or speaker, fifty-six groups in all.
these texts were chanted from memory before being written down
so tradition says; lists and numbers helped monks carry them.

games.q: you need to pass on thousands of teachings, by memory alone, for centuries. how might you sort them?
o: by theme, and by number of items.
by the date each was given.
games.why: the Connected Sayings sort by theme, the Numbered Sayings by number. both are ways to make a huge body of teaching memorable.

practice: Let the Connected Sayings pass by: the flood, the tangle, one arrow, foam on the river, the burden, all is burning, inspired then calm, even his.

Then let the Numbered Sayings pass: remember me as awake, for self and others, heir to my deeds, eight winds, toward less, sleep in peace, a friend gives the hard thing. Hold one line from each book together for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: samyutta. The Pali word for connected or joined together, naming the Samyutta Nikaya: along with the Anguttara Nikaya, sorted by number, thousands of short discourses made to be remembered. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali samyutta: connected, joined together; the Samyutta Nikaya is the 'connected' collection.

carryVoice: Your line: by kind and by number. Tomorrow a new part opens: the festival year. See you there.
